questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is executing uniform circular motion with velocity $\vec{v}$ and acceleration $\vec{a}$. Which of the following is true?
options: $\vec{v}$ is a constant; $\vec{a}$ is a constant
$\vec{v}$ is not a constant; $\vec{a}$ is a constant
$\vec{v}$ is a constant; $\vec{a}$ is not a constant
$\vec{v}$ is not a constant; $\vec{a}$ is not a constant
questions.solution:
$\vec{v}$ is not a constant; $\vec{a}$ is not a constant
In uniform circular motion $\vec{v}$ keeps changing at every instant while magnitude of a remains same but its direction keeps changing.
Thus $\vec{a}$ is also not constant.

From third equation of motion for circular motion

where, $\omega=$ final angular velocity of particle

$\alpha=$ angular acceleration and
$\theta=$ angular displacement
Here, $\omega=\frac{\mathrm{v}_0}{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ (where, $\mathrm{r}$ radius of the circle)

$\theta=2 \pi n$ (for $n$ rounds)

\left(\frac{\mathrm{v}_0}{\mathrm{r}}\right)^2-0=2 \alpha(2 \pi \mathrm{n}) \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{\mathrm{v}_0^2}{4 \pi \mathrm{nr}^2} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}^2

questions.q: A particle is projected up from a point at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal direction. At any time $t$, if $p$ is the linear momentum, $y$ is the vertical displacement, $x$ is horizontal displacement, the graph among the following which does not represent the variation of kinetic energy KE of the particle is
questions.solution:
Momentum, $\quad p=m \cdot v$
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad v=\left(\frac{p}{m}\right) \\ & \text { Kinetic energy, } \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{p^2}{m^2}\right)=\frac{1}{2 m} p^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{KE} \propto p^2 \quad\left(\because \frac{1}{2 m}=\text { constant }\right) \\ & \end{aligned}$ Hence, the graph between KE and $p^2$ will be linear as shown below
Now, kinetic energy KE $=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ The velocity component at point $P$, and $\begin{aligned} & v_y=(u \sin \theta-g t) \\ & v_x=u \cos \theta \end{aligned}$ Resultant velocity at point $P$, $\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}=v_y \hat{\mathbf{j}}+v_x \hat{\mathbf{i}} \\ & =(u \sin \theta-g t) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+u \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{i}} \\ & |\overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}|=\sqrt{(u \cos \theta)^2+(u \sin \theta-g t)^2} \\ & =\sqrt{u^2 \cos ^2 \theta+u^2 \sin ^2 \theta+g^2 t^2-2 u g t \sin \theta} \\ & \therefore=\sqrt{u^2\left(\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta\right)+g^2 t^2-2 u g t \sin \theta} \\ & \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(u^2+g^2 t^2-2 u g t \sin \theta\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{KE} \propto t^2 \\ & \end{aligned}$ Hence, graph will be parabolic with intercept on $y$-axis. Hence, the graph between KE and $t$
Now, in case of height $\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(v^2\right)$ and $v^2=\left(u^2-2 g y\right)\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(u^2-2 g y\right) \\ \mathrm{KE} & =-m g \mathrm{y}+\frac{1}{2} m u^2 \end{aligned}$ Intercept on $y$-axis $=\frac{1}{2} m u^2$ Now, $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$
Now, $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$
$\mathrm{KE} \propto x^2$. Thus graph between KE and $x$ will be parabolic.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected up from a point at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal direction. At any time $t$, if $p$ is the linear momentum, $y$ is the vertical displacement, $x$ is horizontal displacement, the graph among the following which does not represent the variation of kinetic energy KE of the particle is
questions.solution:
Momentum, $\quad p=m \cdot v$
$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad v=\left(\frac{p}{m}\right) \\ & \text { Kinetic energy, } \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{p^2}{m^2}\right)=\frac{1}{2 m} p^2 \\ & \Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{KE} \propto p^2 \quad\left(\because \frac{1}{2 m}=\text { constant }\right) \\ & \end{aligned}$ Hence, the graph between KE and $p^2$ will be linear as shown below
Now, kinetic energy KE $=\frac{1}{2} m v^2$ The velocity component at point $P$, and $\begin{aligned} & v_y=(u \sin \theta-g t) \\ & v_x=u \cos \theta \end{aligned}$ Resultant velocity at point $P$, $\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}=v_y \hat{\mathbf{j}}+v_x \hat{\mathbf{i}} \\ & =(u \sin \theta-g t) \hat{\mathbf{j}}+u \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{i}} \\ & |\overrightarrow{\mathbf{v}}|=\sqrt{(u \cos \theta)^2+(u \sin \theta-g t)^2} \\ & =\sqrt{u^2 \cos ^2 \theta+u^2 \sin ^2 \theta+g^2 t^2-2 u g t \sin \theta} \\ & \therefore=\sqrt{u^2\left(\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta\right)+g^2 t^2-2 u g t \sin \theta} \\ & \mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(u^2+g^2 t^2-2 u g t \sin \theta\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{KE} \propto t^2 \\ & \end{aligned}$ Hence, graph will be parabolic with intercept on $y$-axis. Hence, the graph between KE and $t$
Now, in case of height $\mathrm{KE}=\frac{1}{2} m\left(v^2\right)$ and $v^2=\left(u^2-2 g y\right)\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(u^2-2 g y\right) \\ \mathrm{KE} & =-m g \mathrm{y}+\frac{1}{2} m u^2 \end{aligned}$ Intercept on $y$-axis $=\frac{1}{2} m u^2$ Now, $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$
Now, $\begin{aligned} \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ \mathrm{KE} & =\frac{1}{2} m\left(\frac{x}{t}\right)^2 \end{aligned}$
$\mathrm{KE} \propto x^2$. Thus graph between KE and $x$ will be parabolic.

Reason (R) The range of a projectile depends only on the angle of projection.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of \((A)\).
Both (A) and (R) are true but \((R)\) is not the correct explanation of \((A)\).
questions.solution:

Hence, the range of projectile depends on the angle of projection \(\theta\) and initial velocity \(u\).
\(\therefore\) (A) \(\rightarrow\) True
(B) \(\rightarrow\) False

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : If in a projectile motion, we take air friction into consideration, then \(t_{\text {ascent }} \lt  t_{\text {descent }}\).
Reason : During ascent magnitude of retardation is greater than magnitude of acceleration during descent.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Both the assertion and the reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
- Reasoning for Assertion: In projectile motion with air friction, the opposing drag force acts in the same direction as gravity during ascent, increasing the net downward acceleration (\(\left.a_{\text {ascent }}=g+a_{\text {friction }}\right)\). During descent, the drag force opposes gravity, reducing the net acceleration (\(a_{\text {descent }}=g-a_{\text {friction }}\)). Because the acceleration is greater on the way up, the time to reach the peak (\(t_{\text {ascent }}\)) is shorter than the time to fall back down (\(t_{\text {descent }}\)). Thus, the assertion (\(t_{\text {ascent }}\lt t_{\text {descent }}\)) is true.
- Reasoning for Reason: As explained above, the net downward acceleration during ascent (\(\left.g+a_{\text {friction }}\right)\) is greater in magnitude than the net downward acceleration during descent (\(\left.g-a_{\text {friction }}\right)\). This means the magnitude of retardation on the way up is greater than the magnitude of acceleration on the way down. Thus, the reason is also true.
- Conclusion: The greater retardation during ascent is precisely why the time of ascent is shorter than the time of descent. Therefore, the reason correctly explains the assertion. This corresponds to option (1).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : In case of projectile motion, the magnitude of rate of change of velocity is variable.
Reason : In projectile motion, magnitude of velocity first decreases and then increases during the motion.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
(A) Assertion Analysis
The assertion states that the magnitude of the rate of change of velocity in projectile motion is variable. The rate of change of velocity is acceleration. In projectile motion, acceleration is due to gravity (\(g\)) and is constant. Therefore, the assertion is false.
(B) Reason Analysis
The reason states that the magnitude of velocity first decreases and then increases. As the projectile rises, the vertical component of velocity decreases, causing the overall speed to decrease. At the peak, speed is minimum. As it falls, the vertical component of velocity increases, causing the overall speed to increase. Thus, the reason is true.
Conclusion
The assertion is false, but the reason is true. This corresponds to option (4).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : In case of projectile motion, the magnitude of rate of change of velocity is variable.
Reason : In projectile motion, magnitude of velocity first decreases and then increases during the motion.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Solution: The assertion is false, and the reason is true.
- Assertion: The rate of change of velocity is acceleration. In projectile motion, ignoring air resistance, the acceleration is due to gravity (\(g\)), which is constant. Therefore, the magnitude of the rate of change of velocity is constant, not variable. So, the assertion is false.
- Reason: The magnitude of velocity (speed) in projectile motion is given by \(|v|=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\). The horizontal velocity (\(v_x\)) is constant, but the vertical velocity (\(v_y\)) first decreases to zero at the peak and then increases. This causes the overall speed to decrease on the way up and increase on the way down. So, the reason is true.
The correct option is (4), "If Assertion is false but Reason is true."

Assertion ; In projectile motion, the angle between instantaneous velocity vector and acceleration vector can be anything between 0 to \(\pi\) (excluding the limiting case.)
Reason : In projectile motion, acceleration vector is always pointing vertically downwards. (Neglect air friction).
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, and the reason is the correct explanation of the assertion.
The Reason is true because, neglecting air friction, the only force on a projectile is gravity, which causes a constant downward acceleration.
The Assertion is true because the velocity vector's direction constantly changes, while the acceleration vector remains fixed. This causes the angle between them to continuously vary from a large angle (obtuse) on the way up to a small angle (acute) on the way down, passing through 90 degrees at the peak. The reason explains this variation.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : For projection angle \(\tan ^{-1}(4)\), the horizontal and maximum height of a projectile are equal.
Reason : The maximum range of projectile is directly proportional to square of velocity and inversely proportional to acceleration due to gravity.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
- Assertion: The assertion states that for a projection angle of \(\tan ^{-1}(4)\), the horizontal range (\(R\)) and the maximum height (\(H\)) are equal. This statement is true.
The formulas for range and maximum height are:
\(R=\frac{u^2 \sin (2 \theta)}{g} \text { and } H=\frac{u^2 \sin ^2 \theta}{2 g}\)
For \(R=H\), we set the equations equal to each other:
\(\begin{aligned}
& \frac{u^2 \sin (2 \theta)}{g}=\frac{u^2 \sin ^2 \theta}{2 g} \\
& 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta=\frac{\sin ^2 \theta}{2} \\
& 4 \cos \theta=\sin \theta \\
& \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta}=4 \\
& \tan \theta=4 \\
& \theta=\tan ^{-1}(4)
\end{aligned}\)
This confirms the assertion is correct.
- Reason: The reason states that the maximum range of a projectile is directly proportional to the square of the velocity and inversely proportional to the acceleration due to gravity. The formula for the maximum range is \(R_{\text {max }}=\frac{u^2}{g}\). This is obtained when the projection angle \(\theta=45^{\circ}\). This formula shows that \(R_{\text {max }}\) is directly proportional to the square of the initial velocity (\(u^2\)) and inversely proportional to the acceleration due to gravity (\(g\)). Thus, the reason is true.
Conclusion
Both the Assertion and the Reason are correct. However, the reason discusses the maximum range and its dependencies, while the assertion is about the condition for any range to be equal to the height. The reason, therefore, is a correct statement about projectile motion but does not explain the specific condition in the assertion. This corresponds to option (2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : In projectile motion if time of flight is 4 s. Then, maximum height will be \(20 \mathrm{~m} .\left(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)\)
Reason : Maximum height \(=\frac{g T}{2}\).
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Assertion and Reason Analysis
- Assertion: The assertion states that if the time of flight (\(T\)) is 4 s, the maximum height (\(H\)) is 20 m. We can verify this using the relationship between maximum height and time of flight. The time to reach the maximum height is half the total time of flight, so \(t_{\text {ascent }}=T / 2= 4 / 2=2 \mathrm{~s}\). Using the equation for displacement under constant acceleration:
\(H=u t_{\text {ascent }}+\frac{1}{2} a t_{\text {ascent }}^2\)
The initial vertical velocity component is \(u_y=g \times t_{\text {ascent }}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \times 2 \mathrm{~s}=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\).
Substituting the values:
\(H=(20)(2)+\frac{1}{2}(-10)(2)^2=40-20=20 \mathrm{~m} .\)
Alternatively, using the relationship \(H=\frac{g T^2}{8}\) :
\(H=\frac{(10)(4)^2}{8}=\frac{10 \times 16}{8}=\frac{160}{8}=20 \mathrm{~m} .\)
The assertion is true.
- Reason: The reason claims that the maximum height is \(H=\frac{g T}{2}\). This formula is incorrect. As shown in the assertion analysis, the correct formula is \(H=\frac{g T^2}{8}\). Therefore, the reason is false.
Conclusion
The assertion is true, but the reason is false. This corresponds to option (3).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Assertion : Particle-1 is dropped from a tower and particle-2 is projected horizontal from the same tower. Then, both the particles reach the ground simultaneously.
Reason : Both the particles strike the ground with different speeds.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
If Assertion is true but Reason is false.
If Assertion is false but Reason is true.
questions.solution:
Both the Assertion and the Reason are correct, but the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion.
- Assertion: This statement is true. The time for an object to fall a given vertical distance is determined only by its initial vertical velocity and gravitational acceleration. Since both particles start with zero vertical velocity and fall from the same height, they take the same time to hit the ground.
- Reason: This statement is also true. Particle 1, which is dropped, only has a final vertical velocity (\(v_y\)). Particle 2, which is projected horizontally, has both a final vertical velocity and a constant horizontal velocity \(\left(v_x\right)\). Its final speed is \(\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\), which is greater than the speed of particle 1.
The reason correctly states a fact, but this fact does not explain why the particles land simultaneously. Therefore, option (2) is the correct choice.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
The equation of motion of a projectile is $y=a x-b x^2$, where $a, b$ are constants. Match the column - I with column - II
$\begin{array}{ll}
\text{Column - I} & \text{Column - II} \\
\text{i) The initial velocity of projection} & \text{a)} \frac{a}{b} \\
\text{ii) The horizontal range of projectile} & \text{b)} a \sqrt{\frac{2}{\mathrm{bg}}} \\
\text{iii) The maximum height attained by projectile} & \text{c)} \frac{\mathrm{a}^2}{4 \mathrm{~b}} \\
\text{iv) The time of flight of projectile} & \text{d)} \sqrt{\frac{g\left(1+a^2\right)}{2 b}}
\end{array}$
options: $\begin{array}{cccc}\text { i } & \text { ii } & \text { iii } & \text { iv } \\ \text { a } & \text { d } & \text { c } & \text { b }\end{array}$
questions.solution:
Matching the Columns
i) The initial velocity of projection
From our derivation, \(u=\sqrt{\frac{g\left(1+a^2\right)}{2 b}}\).
This matches option d.
ii) The horizontal range of a projectile
The horizontal range, \(R\), is the value of \(x\) when \(y=0\).
\(y=a x-b x^2=x(a-b x)=0\)
The solutions are \(x=0\) and \(x=\frac{a}{b}\). The range is the non-zero solution.
\(R=\frac{a}{b} .\)
This matches option a.
iii) The maximum height attained by the projectile
The maximum height, \(H\), occurs at the midpoint of the range, so at \(x=R / 2=\frac{a}{2 b}\).
Substitute this into the trajectory equation:
\(H=a\left(\frac{a}{2 b}\right)-b\left(\frac{a}{2 b}\right)^2=\frac{a^2}{2 b}-b\left(\frac{a^2}{4 b^2}\right)=\frac{a^2}{2 b}-\frac{a^2}{4 b}=\frac{2 a^2-a^2}{4 b}=\frac{a^2}{4 b} .\)
This matches option c.
iv) The time of flight of the projectile
The time of flight, \(T\), is related to the range by the horizontal velocity: \(R=u \cos \theta \cdot T\).
\(T=\frac{R}{u \cos \theta}=\frac{a / b}{u / \sqrt{1+\tan ^2 \theta}}=\frac{a}{b} \frac{\sqrt{1+\alpha^2}}{u} .\)
Substitute our expression for \(u\) :
\(T=\frac{a}{b} \frac{\sqrt{1+a^2}}{\sqrt{\frac{\left(1+a^2\right)}{2}}}=\frac{a}{b} \sqrt{\frac{\left(1+a^2\right) 2 b}{g\left(1+a^2\right)}}=\frac{a}{b} \sqrt{\frac{2 b}{g}}=\frac{a \sqrt{2 b}}{b \sqrt{g}}=\frac{a}{b} \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{b} \sqrt{g}}=\frac{a \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{b} \sqrt{g}}=a \sqrt{\frac{2}{b g}} .\)
This matches option b.
Final Matches
- i \(\rightarrow\) d
- ii \(\rightarrow\) a
- iii \(\rightarrow c\)
- iv \(\rightarrow\) b
This matches the configuration of option (3).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A body is projected horizontally from the top of a tower of height $180 \mathrm{~m}$ with a velocity of $20 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. If acceleration due to gravity is $10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$, then match the following.
$\begin{array}{llll}A & B & C & D\end{array}$
questions.solution:
Given, initial horizontal component of velocity,
$u_x=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} \text {. }$
Initial vertical component of velocity,
$u_y=0$
Acceleration due to gravity,
$g=a_y=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$
So, horizontal component of velocity after $1 \mathrm{~s}$,
$\begin{aligned}
v_x & =u_x+a_x t \\
& =20+0=20 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$
and vertical component of velocity after $1 \mathrm{~s}$,
$\begin{aligned}
v_y & =u_y+a_y t \\
& =0+10 \times 1 \\
& =10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}
\end{aligned}$
Horizontal displacement after $1 \mathrm{~s}$,
$\begin{aligned}
s_X & =u_x t+\frac{1}{2} a_X t^2 \\
& =20 \times 1+0=20 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}$
Vertical displacement after $1 \mathrm{~s}$,
$\begin{aligned}
s_y & =u_y t+\frac{1}{2} a_y t^2 \\
& =0+\frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times(1)^2=5 \mathrm{~m}
\end{aligned}$
Resultant velocity after $1 \mathrm{~s}$,
$\begin{aligned}
v= & \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2} \\
= & \sqrt{(20)^2+(10)^2}=\sqrt{400+100}=\sqrt{500} \\
& =22.36=22.4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s},
\end{aligned}$
So, the correct option is (c).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A particle is projected horizontally from a tower with velocity \(10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}\). Taking \(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\). Match the following two columns at time \(t=1 \mathrm{~s}\).
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|}
\hline
& \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\
\hline
(A) & \text{Horizontal component of velocity} & (p) & 5~\text{SI unit} \\
\hline
(B) & \text{Vertical component of velocity} & (q) & 10~\text{SI unit} \\
\hline
(C) & \text{Horizontal displacement} & (r) & 15~\text{SI unit} \\
\hline
(D) & \text{Vertical displacement} & (s) & 20~\text{SI unit} \\
\hline
\end{array}\)
questions.solution:
A) Horizontal component of velocity:
Since there's no horizontal acceleration, the horizontal velocity remains constant.
\(v_x=u_x=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} .\)
This matches (q) 10 SI unit.
B) Vertical component of velocity:
The vertical motion is under constant acceleration due to gravity.
\(v_y=u_y+a_y t=0+(10)(1)=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} .\)
This matches (q) 10 SI unit.
- Note: Both A and B have the same value, which is common in physics problems.
C) Horizontal displacement:
Horizontal displacement is calculated using constant velocity.
\(x=u_x t=(10)(1)=10 \mathrm{~m} .\)
This matches (q) 10 SI unit.
- Note: A, B, and C all have the same value. This confirms our calculations.
D) Vertical displacement:
Vertical displacement is calculated using constant acceleration.
\(y=u_y t+\frac{1}{2} a_y t^2=(0)(1)+\frac{1}{2}(10)(1)^2=0+5=5 \mathrm{~m} .\)
This matches (p) 5 SI unit.
Final Matches
- \(\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}\)
- \(\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}\)
- \(\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{q}\)
- \(\mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}\)
This matches the configuration of option (1).

$\omega_0^2 = \dfrac{(\omega')^2}{2}$

$(\omega')^2 = 2\omega_0^2$

$\omega' = \sqrt{2}\omega_0$.

Answer: $\sqrt{2}\omega_0$

Assertion (A) is incorrect but Reason (R) is correct

The maximum height attained by a projectile is given by the formula $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$, where $u \sin\theta$ is the vertical component of the initial velocity.

This formula does not contain any term for the mass of the projectile. Therefore, in the absence of air resistance, the maximum height is entirely independent of the mass of the body.

Since both stones are projected with the same initial velocity and at the same angle, they have the same vertical component of initial velocity. Thus, they will reach the exact same maximum height.

Assertion (A) is correct. Reason (R) is also correct and provides the exact theoretical justification for why the masses do not affect the maximum height.

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.q: A car is negotiating a flat, unbanked circular turn. For a turn of radius $R$, the maximum safe speed of the car without skidding is $v$. If the radius of the turn is increased to $4R$ while the coefficient of static friction remains the same, what will be the new maximum safe speed for the car?
questions.solution:
The maximum safe speed for a car on a flat circular track is determined by the static friction providing the necessary centripetal force.

Equating the maximum static friction to the required centripetal force:
$\dfrac{mv^2}{R} = \mu mg$

Solving for $v$, we get:
$v = \sqrt{\mu R g}$

This shows that the maximum safe speed is directly proportional to the square root of the radius of the turn ($v \propto \sqrt{R}$).

When the radius is increased to $4R$, the new maximum safe speed $v'$ is:
$v' = \sqrt{\mu (4R) g} = 2\sqrt{\mu R g} = 2v$.

Answer: $2v$

Since the time period $T$ is constant for all particles, the term $\dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ is a constant.
Therefore, $v \propto r$.

The graph of a directly proportional relationship is a straight line passing through the origin.

Answer: A straight line passing through the origin

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A projectile is launched from the ground with an initial speed $u$. At the highest point of its trajectory, its speed is observed to be $\dfrac{u}{2}$. What is the angle of projection of the projectile with the vertical direction?
questions.solution:
Let the angle of projection with the horizontal be $\theta$.

The horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the projectile motion. At the highest point, the vertical component of velocity is zero, so the total speed is just the horizontal component of the velocity.

Speed at highest point, $v = u \cos\theta$

Given that $v = \dfrac{u}{2}$, we have:
$u \cos\theta = \dfrac{u}{2}$
$\Rightarrow \cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$
$\Rightarrow \theta = 60^{\circ}$

The angle of projection with the vertical is $90^{\circ} - \theta = 90^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 30^{\circ}$.

Answer: $30^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A grasshopper leaps from the ground with an initial speed of $2\text{ m/s}$ at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. The maximum vertical height cleared by the grasshopper during its leap is (take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$):
questions.solution:
Given: initial speed $u = 2\text{ m/s}$, angle of projection $\theta = 60^{\circ}$, and $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$.

The maximum height $H$ attained by a projectile is given by the formula:
$H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$

Substitute the given values into the formula:
$\sin 60^{\circ} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$\sin^2 60^{\circ} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$H = \dfrac{(2)^2 \times \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)}{2 \times 10}$
$H = \dfrac{4 \times \dfrac{3}{4}}{20}$
$H = \dfrac{3}{20}\text{ m}$

To convert the height into centimeters, multiply by $100$:
$H = \dfrac{3}{20} \times 100\text{ cm} = 15\text{ cm}$.

Answer: $15\text{ cm}$

questions.q: A ball is thrown at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. If its speed at the maximum height is $15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, what is its initial speed of projection?
questions.solution:
At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, the vertical component of velocity is zero. The speed at this point is entirely due to the horizontal component of the initial velocity, which remains constant throughout the motion.

Let the initial speed be $u$. The speed at the maximum height is given by:
$v = u \cos \theta$

Given that $v = 15 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $\theta = 60^{\circ}$:
$15 = u \cos 60^{\circ}$
$15 = u \times \dfrac{1}{2}$
$u = 30 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $30 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.q: Two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ are moving in concentric circles of radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ respectively. It is given that the ratio of their masses is $m_1 : m_2 = 1 : 2$ and the ratio of their radii is $r_1 : r_2 = 4 : 1$. If they have the same time period of revolution, the ratio of their centripetal forces $F_1 : F_2$ is:
questions.solution:
Time period $T$ is the same for both particles, so their angular velocity $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$ is also the same.

The centripetal force is given by $F = m r \omega^2$.

The ratio of their centripetal forces is:
$\dfrac{F_1}{F_2} = \left(\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}\right) \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right) \left(\dfrac{\omega_1}{\omega_2}\right)^2$

Substitute the given values:
$\dfrac{F_1}{F_2} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{4}{1}\right) \times (1)^2$

$\dfrac{F_1}{F_2} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

Thus, the ratio $F_1 : F_2$ is $2 : 1$.

Answer: $2 : 1$

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A body of mass $m$ is projected from the ground with an initial kinetic energy $K$ at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the vertical. The kinetic energy of the body at the highest point of its trajectory will be
questions.solution:
Let the initial speed of the body be $u$. The initial kinetic energy is given by:
$K = \dfrac{1}{2}mu^2$

The angle of projection with the vertical is $30^{\circ}$. Therefore, the angle of projection with the horizontal is $\theta = 90^{\circ} - 30^{\circ} = 60^{\circ}$.

At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical component of velocity is zero. The speed of the body is equal to the horizontal component of its initial velocity, which remains constant.

Speed at highest point, $v = u \cos 60^{\circ} = u \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{u}{2}$

The kinetic energy at the highest point is:
$K' = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}m\left(\dfrac{u}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}mu^2\right)$

$\Rightarrow K' = \dfrac{K}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{K}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle moves with a constant speed $v$ in a circular path. When the particle covers an angular displacement of $60^{\circ}$, what will be the magnitude of change in its velocity and the change in magnitude of its velocity, respectively?
questions.solution:
Let the initial velocity be $\vec{v}_1$ and final velocity be $\vec{v}_2$.

Since the particle moves with a constant speed $v$, the magnitude of velocity remains constant. Therefore, the change in magnitude of velocity is:
$\Delta |\vec{v}| = |\vec{v}_2| - |\vec{v}_1| = v - v = 0$

The magnitude of change in velocity is given by the vector subtraction of $\vec{v}_1$ from $\vec{v}_2$:
$|\Delta \vec{v}| = |\vec{v}_2 - \vec{v}_1| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 - 2v_1v_2\cos\theta}$

Given $\theta = 60^{\circ}$ and $v_1 = v_2 = v$:
$|\Delta \vec{v}| = \sqrt{v^2 + v^2 - 2(v)(v)\cos 60^{\circ}}$
$|\Delta \vec{v}| = \sqrt{2v^2 - 2v^2 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \sqrt{v^2} = v$

Thus, the magnitude of change in velocity is $v$, and the change in magnitude of velocity is $0$.

Answer: $v, 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two projectiles are fired from the ground with the same initial speed $u$. One is fired at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal, and the other is fired at an angle $(90^\circ - \theta)$ with the horizontal. The sum of their maximum heights is:
questions.solution:
The maximum height of a projectile is given by $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$.

For the first projectile fired at an angle $\theta$:
$H_1 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

For the second projectile fired at an angle $(90^\circ - \theta)$:
$H_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2(90^\circ - \theta)}{2g} = \dfrac{u^2 \cos^2\theta}{2g}$

The sum of their maximum heights is:
$H_1 + H_2 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g} + \dfrac{u^2 \cos^2\theta}{2g}$

$H_1 + H_2 = \dfrac{u^2}{2g} (\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)$

Using the trigonometric identity $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$, we get:
$H_1 + H_2 = \dfrac{u^2}{2g}$

Answer: $\dfrac{u^2}{2g}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A projectile is fired from the surface of the earth with an initial speed of $40 \mathrm{~m/s}$. If its speed at the highest point of its trajectory is exactly half of its initial projection speed, what is the maximum height attained by the projectile? (Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$ and neglect air resistance)
questions.solution:
Let the initial speed be $u$ and the angle of projection with the horizontal be $\theta$.

At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero, and the projectile only has a horizontal component of velocity, which remains constant throughout the motion. Thus, the speed at the highest point is $v = u \cos\theta$.

Given that the speed at the highest point is half of the initial speed:
$u \cos\theta = \dfrac{u}{2}$
$\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \implies \theta = 60^{\circ}$

The maximum height $H$ is given by the formula:
$H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

Substituting $u = 40 \mathrm{~m/s}$, $\theta = 60^{\circ}$, and $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$:
$H = \dfrac{(40)^2 \times (\sin 60^{\circ})^2}{2 \times 10}$
$H = \dfrac{1600 \times \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2}{20}$
$H = \dfrac{1600 \times \dfrac{3}{4}}{20} = \dfrac{1200}{20} = 60 \mathrm{~m}$

Answer: $60 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is projected from the ground with a speed of $40 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ at an angle of $30^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. What is the magnitude of the change in its velocity between the point of projection and the highest point of its trajectory?
questions.solution:
Let the point of projection be the origin. The initial velocity vector $\vec{u}$ can be resolved into horizontal and vertical components:

$\vec{u} = u \cos \theta \hat{i} + u \sin \theta \hat{j}$

$\vec{u} = 40 \cos 30^{\circ} \hat{i} + 40 \sin 30^{\circ} \hat{j} = 20\sqrt{3} \hat{i} + 20 \hat{j} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

At the highest point of the trajectory, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero, while the horizontal component remains constant.

Velocity at the highest point, $\vec{v} = 20\sqrt{3} \hat{i} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The change in velocity vector is $\Delta \vec{v} = \vec{v} - \vec{u}$

$\Delta \vec{v} = (20\sqrt{3} \hat{i}) - (20\sqrt{3} \hat{i} + 20 \hat{j}) = -20 \hat{j} \text{ m s}^{-1}$

The magnitude of the change in velocity is $|\Delta \vec{v}| = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is thrown such that its horizontal range is exactly $4\sqrt{3}$ times its maximum height. The angle of projection with the horizontal is:
questions.solution:
The horizontal range $R$ and maximum height $H$ of a projectile are given by:

$R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g} = \dfrac{u^2 (2 \sin\theta \cos\theta)}{g}$

$H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

According to the given condition, $R = 4\sqrt{3} H$. Substituting the formulas:

$\dfrac{u^2 (2 \sin\theta \cos\theta)}{g} = 4\sqrt{3} \left( \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g} \right)$

Cancelling $\dfrac{u^2}{g}$ from both sides:

$2 \sin\theta \cos\theta = 2\sqrt{3} \sin^2\theta$

Assuming $\theta \neq 0$, we can divide both sides by $2 \sin\theta \cos\theta$:

$1 = \sqrt{3} \tan\theta$

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

$\theta = 30^{\circ}$

Answer: $30^{\circ}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder and a uniform solid sphere, having the same mass and the same radius, are free to rotate about their respective central axes. If the same constant torque is applied to both for the same time duration starting from rest, what will be the ratio of the final angular velocity of the solid cylinder to that of the solid sphere?
questions.solution:
Let the mass of both objects be $M$ and their radius be $R$.

The moment of inertia of a uniform solid cylinder about its central axis is $I_{cyl} = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2$.

The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about its central axis is $I_{sph} = \dfrac{2}{5}MR^2$.

From Newton's second law for rotation, the angular acceleration is given by $\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I}$.

Since both objects start from rest, their final angular velocity after time $t$ is $\omega = \alpha t = \dfrac{\tau t}{I}$.

Given that the applied torque $\tau$ and time $t$ are the same for both, the angular velocity is inversely proportional to the moment of inertia ($\omega \propto \dfrac{1}{I}$).

Therefore, the ratio of their angular velocities is:
$\dfrac{\omega_{cyl}}{\omega_{sph}} = \dfrac{I_{sph}}{I_{cyl}} = \dfrac{\dfrac{2}{5}MR^2}{\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2} = \dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{2}{1} = \dfrac{4}{5}$

The ratio is $4 : 5$.

Answer: $4 : 5$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A stone is dropped from the roof of a building. It is observed to pass a window of height $2.0\text{ m}$ in $0.2\text{ s}$. (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$). Consider the following statements:

(I) The velocity of the stone at the top edge of the window is $9\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
(II) The velocity of the stone at the bottom edge of the window is $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
(III) The top edge of the window is $4.05\text{ m}$ below the roof.
(IV) The stone takes $0.5\text{ s}$ to reach the top edge of the window from the roof.

How many of the above statements are correct?
questions.solution:
Let us evaluate each statement by analyzing the motion of the stone.

For the motion across the window:
Displacement $s = 2.0\text{ m}$
Time $t = 0.2\text{ s}$
Acceleration $a = g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$

Using the second equation of motion to find the velocity at the top edge ($u$):
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$
$2.0 = u(0.2) + \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(0.2)^2$
$2.0 = 0.2u + 5(0.04)$
$2.0 = 0.2u + 0.2$
$1.8 = 0.2u \Rightarrow u = 9\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Thus, statement (I) is correct.

Velocity at the bottom edge of the window ($v$):
$v = u + at = 9 + 10(0.2) = 9 + 2 = 11\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Thus, statement (II) is incorrect.

For the motion from the roof to the top edge of the window (initial velocity $= 0$):
Using $v^2 = u^2 + 2gh$, where $v = 9\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $u = 0$:
$9^2 = 0 + 2(10)h$
$81 = 20h \Rightarrow h = 4.05\text{ m}$.
Thus, statement (III) is correct.

Time taken to reach the top edge from the roof:
Using $v = u + gt$
$9 = 0 + 10t \Rightarrow t = 0.9\text{ s}$.
Thus, statement (IV) is incorrect.

Exactly two statements, (I) and (III), are correct.

Answer: Two

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two identical balls, A and B, are projected with the same initial speed. Ball A is projected at an angle of $30^\circ$ with the horizontal, while ball B is projected at an angle of $30^\circ$ with the vertical. The ratio of the speed of ball A to the speed of ball B at their respective highest points is
questions.solution:
For ball A, the angle of projection with the horizontal is $\theta_A = 30^\circ$.

Speed of ball A at the highest point is its horizontal component of velocity:
$v_A = u \cos 30^\circ = u \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$

For ball B, the angle of projection with the vertical is $30^\circ$, so its angle with the horizontal is $\theta_B = 90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$.

Speed of ball B at the highest point is:
$v_B = u \cos 60^\circ = u \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$

The ratio of their speeds at the highest points is:
$\dfrac{v_A}{v_B} = \dfrac{u \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}{u \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1}$

Therefore, the ratio is $\sqrt{3} : 1$.

Answer: $\sqrt{3} : 1$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A particle is executing uniform circular motion. Match the kinematic quantities in List-I with their corresponding properties in List-II.

List-IList-II
A. VelocityI. Constant scalar
B. SpeedII. Constant vector
C. Tangential accelerationIII. Changing vector
D. Angular velocityIV. Zero vector

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
In uniform circular motion, the particle moves with a constant speed. Thus, speed is a constant scalar.

The direction of motion changes continuously along the circular path, meaning the velocity vector changes its direction at every point. Hence, velocity is a changing vector.

Tangential acceleration is the rate of change of speed. Since speed is constant, the tangential acceleration is zero, making it a zero vector.

Angular velocity is given by the right-hand thumb rule and points along the axis of rotation. In uniform circular motion, both its magnitude and direction remain constant. Thus, angular velocity is a constant vector.

Therefore, the correct matching is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

Answer: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two particles are moving in uniform circular motion in circles of radii $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$. If they experience the exact same magnitude of centripetal acceleration, the ratio of their time periods of revolution ($T_{1}:T_{2}$) will be:
questions.solution:
The centripetal acceleration of a particle in uniform circular motion is given by $a_{c} = \omega^{2}r$.

Since $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$, we can write $a_{c} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{T^{2}}r$.

Given that the centripetal accelerations are equal ($a_{c1} = a_{c2}$):

$\dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{T_{1}^{2}}R_{1} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{T_{2}^{2}}R_{2}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{T_{1}^{2}}{T_{2}^{2}} = \dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{T_{1}}{T_{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{R_{1}}{R_{2}}}$

Thus, the ratio of their time periods is $\sqrt{R_{1}}:\sqrt{R_{2}}$.

Answer: $\sqrt{R_{1}}:\sqrt{R_{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A stone dropped from a helicopter passes a tall vertical glass building. It takes $2\text{ s}$ to cross the entire height of the building. The velocity of the stone at the bottom of the building is exactly three times its velocity at the top of the building. Find the height of the building. (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the velocity of the stone at the top of the building be $u$.

The velocity at the bottom of the building is given as $v = 3u$.

Using the first equation of motion, $v = u + gt$ for the motion across the building:
$3u = u + (10)(2)$
$2u = 20 \Rightarrow u = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}$

Now, use the second equation of motion to find the height of the building ($s$):
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$
$s = (10)(2) + \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(2)^2$
$s = 20 + 20 = 40\text{ m}$

Answer: $40\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For an oblique projectile fired from the ground, the minimum speed during its flight is equal to the horizontal component of its initial velocity.

Reason (R): The vertical component of velocity becomes zero at the highest point, while the horizontal component remains unchanged throughout the flight.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false but Reason (R) is true.
questions.solution:
The velocity of an oblique projectile at any instant is the vector sum of its horizontal and vertical components.

The horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight because there is no horizontal acceleration.

The vertical component of velocity decreases as the projectile ascends, becomes zero at the highest point, and then increases downwards.

Since the total speed is $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2}$, it will be minimum when $v_y = 0$.

This happens at the highest point, where the speed is simply $v_x$, which is the horizontal component of the initial velocity. Thus, Assertion (A) is true.

Reason (R) correctly states that the vertical component becomes zero at the highest point and the horizontal component is unchanged, which perfectly explains why the minimum speed is the horizontal component.

Therefore, both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

Answer: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniform solid disc of mass $4 \text{ kg}$ and radius $0.5 \text{ m}$ is pivoted at its centre and is initially at rest. A constant tangential force of $10 \text{ N}$ is applied to its rim. What will be the angular velocity of the disc after $3 \text{ s}$?
questions.solution:
The moment of inertia of a uniform solid disc about its central axis is:
$I = \dfrac{1}{2}MR^2 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (0.5)^2 = 2 \times 0.25 = 0.5 \text{ kg m}^2$

The torque produced by the tangential force applied at the rim is:
$\tau = F \times R = 10 \times 0.5 = 5 \text{ N m}$

Using Newton's second law for rotation, the angular acceleration $\alpha$ is:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{5}{0.5} = 10 \text{ rad/s}^2$

Since the disc starts from rest ($\omega_i = 0$), the final angular velocity after $t = 3 \text{ s}$ is:
$\omega_f = \omega_i + \alpha t = 0 + (10 \times 3) = 30 \text{ rad/s}$

Answer: $30 \text{ rad/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two athletes are running on concentric circular tracks of radii $R$ and $2R$. They start simultaneously and complete one full lap at the exact same instant. The ratio of their linear speeds is:
questions.solution:
Since both athletes complete one full lap in the same time, their time periods $T$ are equal.

Angular speed is given by $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$. Since $T$ is the same, $\omega$ is the same for both athletes.

The linear speed is related to angular speed by $v = \omega r$.

Therefore, the ratio of their linear speeds is $\dfrac{v_{1}}{v_{2}} = \dfrac{\omega R}{\omega (2R)} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, which is $1:2$.

Answer: $1:2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is dropped from rest from the top of a tall cliff. In the last $1\text{ s}$ of its fall before hitting the ground, it covers a distance of $45\text{ m}$. What is the total height of the cliff? (Take $g = 10\text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
Let the velocity of the ball $1\text{ s}$ before hitting the ground be $u$.

For the last $1\text{ s}$ of the fall, the distance covered is $45\text{ m}$. Using the second equation of motion:
$s = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$
$45 = u(1) + \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(1)^2$
$45 = u + 5 \Rightarrow u = 40\text{ m s}^{-1}$

This velocity $u = 40\text{ m s}^{-1}$ is attained by the ball after falling from rest. Let the time taken to reach this velocity be $t_1$.
Using $v = u_{initial} + gt_1$:
$40 = 0 + 10t_1 \Rightarrow t_1 = 4\text{ s}$

The total time of fall is the time taken to reach $40\text{ m s}^{-1}$ plus the last $1\text{ s}$:
$t_{total} = 4 + 1 = 5\text{ s}$

The total height of the cliff $H$ is the distance fallen from rest in $5\text{ s}$:
$H = \dfrac{1}{2}gt_{total}^2$
$H = \dfrac{1}{2}(10)(5)^2 = 5 \times 25 = 125\text{ m}$

Answer: $125\text{ m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A grindstone of moment of inertia $5 \text{ kg m}^2$ is rotating at $600 \text{ rpm}$. A constant retarding torque of $10\pi \text{ N m}$ is applied to it. The number of complete revolutions the grindstone makes before coming to rest is
questions.solution:
Given, initial angular velocity $\omega_i = 600 \text{ rpm} = 600 \times \dfrac{2\pi}{60} \text{ rad/s} = 20\pi \text{ rad/s}$
Final angular velocity $\omega_f = 0$
Moment of inertia $I = 5 \text{ kg m}^2$
Retarding torque $\tau = 10\pi \text{ N m}$

The angular deceleration $\alpha$ is:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\tau}{I} = \dfrac{10\pi}{5} = 2\pi \text{ rad/s}^2$

Using the third equation of rotational kinematics:
$\omega_f^2 = \omega_i^2 - 2\alpha\theta$
$0 = (20\pi)^2 - 2(2\pi)\theta$
$4\pi\theta = 400\pi^2$
$\theta = 100\pi \text{ rad}$

The number of complete revolutions $n$ is:
$n = \dfrac{\theta}{2\pi} = \dfrac{100\pi}{2\pi} = 50$

Answer: $50$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The equation of trajectory of a projectile is given by $y = x - 5x^2$, where $x$ and $y$ are the horizontal and vertical displacements respectively, measured in meters. The maximum height attained by the projectile is:
questions.solution:
The equation of the trajectory is $y = x - 5x^2$.

The maximum height corresponds to the maximum value of the vertical displacement $y$. To find the maximum value of $y$, we differentiate $y$ with respect to $x$ and set it to zero:
$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 - 10x = 0$
$\implies 10x = 1 \implies x = 0.1 \mathrm{~m}$

This means the projectile reaches its maximum height at a horizontal distance of $x = 0.1 \mathrm{~m}$.

To find the maximum height, substitute $x = 0.1 \mathrm{~m}$ back into the trajectory equation:
$y_{\text{max}} = (0.1) - 5(0.1)^2$
$y_{\text{max}} = 0.1 - 5(0.01)$
$y_{\text{max}} = 0.1 - 0.05 = 0.05 \mathrm{~m}$

Alternatively, comparing $y = x - 5x^2$ with the standard trajectory equation $y = x \tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2 \cos^2\theta}$, we get $\tan\theta = 1 \implies \theta = 45^{\circ}$.
The second term gives $\dfrac{g}{2u^2 \cos^2(45^{\circ})} = 5 \implies \dfrac{10}{2u^2 (1/2)} = 5 \implies \dfrac{10}{u^2} = 5 \implies u^2 = 2$.
Then, maximum height $H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g} = \dfrac{2 \times (1/\sqrt{2})^2}{2 \times 10} = \dfrac{1}{20} = 0.05 \mathrm{~m}$.

Answer: $0.05 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A projectile is launched with an initial speed $u$ such that its horizontal range is exactly equal to its maximum height. What is the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its trajectory?
questions.solution:
The horizontal range $R$ and maximum height $H$ of a projectile are given by:
$R = \dfrac{u^2 \sin 2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2u^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g}$
$H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$

Given that $R = H$:
$\dfrac{2u^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta}{g} = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2 \theta}{2g}$

Simplifying this gives:
$2 \cos \theta = \dfrac{\sin \theta}{2}$
$\tan \theta = 4$

From $\tan \theta = 4$, we can find $\cos \theta$ using a right-angled triangle with opposite side $4$ and adjacent side $1$. The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{4^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{17}$.
Thus, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}}$.

The speed at the highest point is the horizontal component of the initial velocity, as the vertical component becomes zero:
$v = u \cos \theta = \dfrac{u}{\sqrt{17}}$

Answer: $\dfrac{u}{\sqrt{17}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A particle executing uniform circular motion possesses a constant linear acceleration.
Reason (R): In uniform circular motion, the acceleration vector always points towards the center of the circular path, meaning its direction continuously changes.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are correct but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A)
Assertion (A) is correct but Reason (R) is not correct
Assertion (A) is not correct but Reason (R) is correct
questions.solution:
In uniform circular motion, the speed of the particle is constant, but its direction of motion changes continuously. The linear acceleration (centripetal acceleration) is directed towards the center of the circular path. As the particle moves along the circle, the direction towards the center continuously changes in space. Since acceleration is a vector quantity, a change in its direction means the acceleration is varying, not constant. Therefore, Assertion (A) is not correct.

Reason (R) correctly states that the acceleration vector points towards the center and its direction continuously changes, which is a true statement.

Answer: Assertion (A) is not correct but Reason (R) is correct

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A bullet fired horizontally into a thick wooden block undergoes uniform deceleration. It takes $0.1\text{ s}$ to travel through the first $30\text{ cm}$ of the block, and its velocity at the end of this $30\text{ cm}$ is exactly half of its entry velocity. What is the entry velocity of the bullet?
questions.solution:
Let the entry velocity of the bullet be $u$ and the final velocity after travelling $30\text{ cm}$ be $v$.

Given:
Distance $s = 30\text{ cm} = 0.3\text{ m}$
Time $t = 0.1\text{ s}$
Final velocity $v = \dfrac{u}{2}$

For uniformly accelerated (or decelerated) motion, the displacement can be expressed in terms of average velocity:
$s = \left(\dfrac{u + v}{2}\right)t$

Substituting the given values:
$0.3 = \left(\dfrac{u + \dfrac{u}{2}}{2}\right) \times 0.1$

$0.3 = \left(\dfrac{3u}{4}\right) \times 0.1$

$3 = \dfrac{3u}{4}$

$u = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

The entry velocity of the bullet is $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The initial velocity of a projectile is given by $\vec{u} = (6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}) \text{ m s}^{-1}$, where $\hat{i}$ is along the horizontal and $\hat{j}$ is along the vertical direction. What is the speed of the projectile at its maximum height?
questions.solution:
In projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity remains constant throughout the flight, while the vertical component changes due to gravity.

Given the initial velocity vector $\vec{u} = 6\hat{i} + 8\hat{j}$, the horizontal component is $u_x = 6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and the vertical component is $u_y = 8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

At the maximum height, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero ($v_y = 0$).

Therefore, the velocity at the maximum height is entirely horizontal: $\vec{v} = 6\hat{i} \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

The speed at the maximum height is the magnitude of this velocity, which is $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Answer: $6 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A water fountain shoots a stream of water at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ to the horizontal. If the maximum height reached by the water droplets is $15 \text{ m}$, what is the initial speed of the water? (Take $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$)
questions.solution:
The maximum height $H$ of a projectile is given by the formula:

$H = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2\theta}{2g}$

Given that $H = 15 \text{ m}$, $\theta = 60^{\circ}$, and $g = 10 \text{ m s}^{-2}$, we can substitute these values into the formula:

$15 = \dfrac{u^2 \sin^2(60^{\circ})}{2 \times 10}$

Since $\sin(60^{\circ}) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, we have $\sin^2(60^{\circ}) = \dfrac{3}{4}$.

$15 = \dfrac{u^2 \times \dfrac{3}{4}}{20}$

$15 \times 20 = u^2 \times \dfrac{3}{4}$

$300 = u^2 \times \dfrac{3}{4}$

$u^2 = \dfrac{300 \times 4}{3} = 400$

$u = \sqrt{400} = 20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

Answer: $20 \text{ m s}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A particle is moving along a circular path such that its speed is continuously increasing. What will be the nature of the angle between its velocity vector and its net acceleration vector?
questions.solution:
For a particle moving in a circular path with an increasing speed, there are two components of acceleration:
1. Centripetal acceleration ($a_c$), which is directed towards the center of the circle and is perpendicular to the velocity vector.
2. Tangential acceleration ($a_t$), which is responsible for the increase in speed. Since the speed is increasing, $a_t$ is in the same direction as the velocity vector.

The net acceleration ($\vec{a}$) is the vector sum of $\vec{a}_c$ and $\vec{a}_t$. Because $\vec{a}_t$ is parallel to the velocity and $\vec{a}_c$ is perpendicular to it, the resultant net acceleration vector lies between the velocity vector and the centripetal acceleration vector. Therefore, the angle between the velocity vector and the net acceleration vector is greater than $0^{\circ}$ and less than $90^{\circ}$, which means it is an acute angle.

Answer: Acute angle

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a coin is placed on a rotating record player, it is more likely to slip off if it is placed closer to the edge than near the center.
Reason (R): The required centripetal force for a particle moving in a circle of constant radius is directly proportional to the square of its angular velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Assertion and Reason are true and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Assertion is true but Reason is false
Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
For a coin placed on a rotating record player, the angular velocity $\omega$ is the same for all points.

The required centripetal force to prevent slipping is $F_c = m r \omega^2$. As the distance $r$ from the center increases (closer to the edge), the required centripetal force increases. Since the maximum static friction $f_s = \mu m g$ is constant, the coin is more likely to slip at a larger radius. Thus, the Assertion is true.

The Reason states that for a constant radius, $F_c \propto \omega^2$. This is a true statement based on $F_c = m r \omega^2$. However, it does not explain the Assertion, which is based on the variation of $F_c$ with radius $r$ at a constant $\omega$.

Therefore, both Assertion and Reason are true, but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Answer: Both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion

questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} & \text { The time of flight }=\frac{2 u \sin \theta}{g} \\ & =\frac{2 \times 9.8 \times \sin 30^{\circ}}{9.8}=1 \mathrm{~s}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A projectile is thrown in the upward direction making an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal direction with a velocity of $147 \mathrm{~ms}^{-1}$. Then the time after which its inclination with the horizontal is $45^{\circ}$, is
questions.solution:
Key Idea : At the two points of the trajectory during projection, the horizontal component of the velocity is the same.
Horizontal component of velocity at angle $60^{\circ}=$ Horizontal component of velocity at $45^{\circ}i e, \quad u \cos 60^{\circ}=v \sin 45^{\circ}$
or $\quad 147 \times \frac{1}{2}=v \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
or $\quad v=\frac{147}{\sqrt{2}} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
Vertical component of $u=u \sin 60^{\circ}=\frac{147 \sqrt{3}}{2} \mathrm{~m}$
Vertical component of $v=v \sin 45^{\circ}=\frac{147}{\sqrt{2}} \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{147}{2} \mathrm{~m}$
but $\quad v_y=u_y+a t\therefore \quad \frac{147}{2}=\frac{147 \sqrt{3}}{2}-9.8 t$
or $\quad 9.8 t=\frac{147}{2}(\sqrt{3}-1)\therefore \quad t=5.49 \mathrm{~s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A river is flowing from west to east with a speed of $5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{min}$. A man can swim in still water with a velocity $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{min}$. In which direction should the man swim so, as to take the shortest possible path to go to the south?
questions.solution: Let the swimmer swims at an angle $\theta$ with the vertical. $\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \sin \theta & =\frac{v_r}{v_s}=\frac{5}{10}=\frac{1}{2}=\sin 30^{\circ} \\ \theta & =30^{\circ}\end{aligned}$ The swimmer should swim $30^{\circ}$ east of south to take the shortest possible path to go to the south.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward. It has a speed of $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ when it has reached one-half of its maximum height. How high does the ball rise? (Take, $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ )
questions.solution: The problem can be solved using third equation of motion at $A$ and $O$ '. Let maximum height attained by the ball be H.Third equation of motion gives $v^2=u^2-2 g h$ At $A$, $(10)^2=u^2-2 \times 10 \times \frac{H}{2}\Rightarrow u^2=100+10 H...(i)$ At $O^{\prime},(0)^2=u^2-2 \times 10 \times H\Rightarrow u^2=20 H...(ii)$ Thus, from Eqs. (i) and (ii), we get $20 H=100+10 H\Rightarrow 10 H=100 \quad \therefore H=10 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.q: A stone is thrown with an initial speed of $4.9 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ from a bridge in vertically upward direction. It falls down in water after 2 sec . The height of bridge is
questions.solution:
Here: Initial velocity $u=-4.9 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ (- ve is due to vertically upward motion)
Total time $t=2 \mathrm{sec}$
The height of the bridge is given by
$s=u t+\frac{1}{2} g t^2\begin{aligned} & =-4.9 \times 2+\frac{1}{2} \times 9.8 \times(2)^2 \\ & =-9.8+19.6=9.8 \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The maximum range of a gun on horizontal terrain is 16 km , if $g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$. What must be the muzzle velocity of the shell?
questions.solution:
We know that in projection of the particle, for maximum range, $\theta=45^{\circ}$
Now maximum range
$\begin{aligned} & R=\frac{u^2 \sin 2 \theta}{g}=\frac{u^2 \sin 90^{\circ}}{g} \\ & u=\sqrt{R g} & ...(1) \end{aligned}$
Here : $R_{\max }=16 \mathrm{~km}=16 \times 10^3 \mathrm{~m}$,
$g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$
Now from eq. (1), we get
$u=\sqrt{16 \times 10^3 \times 10}=400 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The earth of mass $=6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$ revolves around the sun with an angular velocity of $2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$ in a circular orbit of radius $1.5 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~km}$. The force exerted by the sun on earth is :
questions.solution:
Here: Mass of earth $M_e=6 \times 10^{24} \mathrm{~kg}$
Angular velocity of earth $\omega=2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{s}$
Radius of circular orbit
$\begin{aligned}R & =1.5 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~km} \\& =1.5 \times 10^{11} \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$
Force exerted on the earth by the sun is given by
$\begin{aligned}F & =M_e R \omega^2 \\& =6 \times 10^{24} \times 1.5 \times 10^{11} \times\left(2 \times 10^{-7}\right)^2 \\& =36 \times 10^{21} \mathrm{~N}\end{aligned}$
